column2: What is mine of great-grandfather's father, my great-grandfathers — and he gave to the great-grandfather, with kusha, perfume and sesame mixed with flowers, with the left (apasavya) manner.
Likewise Janardana did the rite for the maternal grandfathers; worshipping them again with perfumes and the rest, he gave incense with devotion.
Reciting "Adityas, Vasus, Rudras," the lord of the world then took food mixed with ghee, sesame and kusha,
placed it in a vessel and asked the sages: "I shall offer in the fire." Told by them "Do so,"
he should give three oblations to Soma, Agni and Yama, and recite the seven Yajus verses beginning "Ye mamaka" to Achyuta.
The remainder of the offering he gave with name and gotra, three oblations for each ancestor, Brahmins.
Then he placed the remaining food in the pinda vessel. Then he gave tasty sweet food, rice-pudding first,
fresh, cooked once, not stale, excellent, with few greens and much fruit, of six flavours, like nectar,
which he gave to the Brahmins and in the pinda vessel to the ancestors, preceded by Vedic recital, the ancestors' food flooded with ghee, sprinkled with honey,
consecrated with "Prithivi"; while the Brahmins ate, he sang the Madhuvata rik and recited the set of five mantras,
beginning with those suitable, no more than that; he recited the Trimadhu, Trisuparna and Brihadaranyaka,
and murmured their japa, the Saura Sukta with the Purusha Sukta. When the Brahmins had eaten, asking "Are you satisfied?"
We are satisfied, they said; he gave water once, releasing from silence. Taking the pinda vessel he then gave it to Chhaya.
She divided that food in two and made it each threefold. Varaha then marking the earth and covering it with kusha,
making the kusha point south, and a seat over them, having refuge on kusha with sesame and with roots,
having made perfume and flowers, then with devotion gave the pinda, saying "Prithivi, sustain."
The grandfathers, great-grandfathers and "So be it," from the sky; thus the boar gave pindas to the maternal grandfathers also.
He gave the food left over from the offering of the pinda to those who eat the smearings; saying "This is for you, father," he gave garments with devotion,
white, washed, new, two fingers' breadth; having given perfumes, flowers and the rest, and circumambulating them,
he should make the Brahmins rinse, first those of the ancestors, then the gods; then sprinkling that ground, giving water, good flowers and unbroken grain,
giving water with sesame to the ancestors first and with unbroken grain to the gods: "May it be imperishable for us," and "Let the deities be pleased";
having pleased them, turning around, he should recite the Aghamarshana three times; then turning back he should recite "Yan me nama".
Ancestors, give us houses filled with wealth and grain. Setting the arghya vessels with purifiers among the pindas,
he murmured "They bear vigour," and the Koka water. He gave libation to the ancestors with cold milk, honey and sesame.
When the ancestral Brahmins said "May it be well," at midday, satisfying again, the god Gadadhara, giving silver as fee to the Brahmins,
gave a share to humans, saying "Svadha." Someone said "Accomplished," and was answered by them, best of Brahmins:
Be content, he said; they said, "We are content." He asked about the remaining food, urged with those desired,
taking those Brahmins by the hand and following them then, reciting "Vaje vaje," he went out of the altar;
with water of Kotitirtha, raising apasavya, he prayed for blessing for the hairs...:
May our givers prosper. They said "So be it." Circumambulating and bowing at their feet,
the boar gave them seats and covered them; "Rest," he said, then entering took the middle pinda.
The lord gave a pinda to his wife Earth, formed of Chhaya, saying "Ancestors, set an embryo"; she too, embodied,
took the pinda and bowed at the feet of the Brahmins. The boar, wishing to dismiss the ancestors,
Koka and the ancestors said words serving their own end: "Revered one, formerly we were cursed by the moon, dwellers in heaven:
'You will all become fallen from yoga, fallen from heaven.' Thus you have saved us as we entered Rasatala.
The lords of the universe, protectors of yoga, abandoned us fallen from yoga; may the Vishvedevas protect you again, always for us.
We shall go to heaven, lord, by your grace, boar; and may Soma be our presiding deity, Achyuta, the bearer of yoga.
Soma, support of yoga, never abandons; may our dwelling be in heaven and on earth always through yoga.
For some in the atmosphere for a month; and for us nourishment; and this Urja, our wife, famed by the name Svadha,
may she be rich in yoga, mother of yoga, sky-goer." Thus addressed by the ancestors, Varaha, source of beings,
then Vishnu said to the ancestors and to the great river Koka: "All that you have said to me will be.
Yama will be your presiding deity; Soma is declared your Vedic study; and fire your sacrificial overlord; this is your conception.
Agni, Vayu and Sun are your place; Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra are your chief persons.
The Adityas, Vasus and Rudras are these your forms. Yogis with yogic bodies, bearers of yoga and of good vows,
you will roam at will, bestowers of fruit upon all beings, upon those in heaven, in hell and on earth, moving and unmoving,
by your own yogic power alone you will gratify, the excellent. This Urja, daughter of the Moon, with a body of nectar and honey,
will be the fortunate Svadha, daughter of Daksha; she, fair-faced, will be your wife there.
She is famed as the river Koka, resting on the king of mountains, of great merit with crores of holy places, protected by my form.
From today I shall dwell in her, destroying sin; seeing Varaha is meritorious, worshipping him grants enjoyment and liberation;
drinking the Koka water destroys great sins; bathing in holy places is meritorious, fasting there gives heaven;
a gift there is declared imperishable, removing birth, death and old age. In the month of Magha, in the dark fortnight, at the waning of the moon,
you should come to Kokamukha and stay five days; and whoever at that time offers shraddha to ancestors
will share the fruit told before, no doubt. I shall always stay here on the eleventh and twelfth;
the wise man who fasts there will get the fruit told earlier. So go, fortunate ones, to the desired place as you wish."
Saying "I too shall live here," he vanished; when Varaha had gone, the ancestors, taking leave of Koka, departed.
Koka too, with the holy place, stayed on the king of mountains; Chhaya, formed of earth, the boar's mate, nourished by eating the pinda,
the beautiful one, with faith, took Varaha's embryo; from her was born the son, Bhauma Narakasura, and the city Pragjyotisha was given to him by Vishnu.
Thus the divine boar form of Vishnu the boon-giver at Kokamukha has been told by me; a man hearing it, free of stain and sin, would obtain the fruit of a ten horse-sacrifice offering.

On the tenth day a Brahmin is purified, on the twelfth a Kshatriya, a Vaishya on the fifteenth, a Shudra purifies in a month.
At the end of the impurity, shraddha at home, called Ekoddishta, on the twelfth day, in the month, and then in the third fortnight,
should be done every month up to a year, Brahmins; after that the Sapindikarana should be done in order.
When Sapindikarana has been done, the Parvana (shraddha) is told again; from then on, freed from ghost-hood, they have reached the state of ancestors.
Ancestors are remembered as twofold, formless and formed; the Nandimukhas are formless, the Parvana ones formed. Those eating Ekoddishta are ghosts: thus the determination of ancestors is threefold.
How is Sapindikarana to be done, best of Brahmins, for one who has become a ghost, by rule? Tell us, best of speakers.

Brahmins, hear the Sapindikarana as I tell: it is without gods, with one arghya and one purifier;
brahmapuran:220:70	no making in fire there; it is without invocation; and there too in the apasavya manner; he should feed an uneven number of Brahmins.
brahmapuran:220:71	There is another special thing there, beginning with the monthly rites; best of Brahmins, hear it as I tell, with one-pointed mind.
brahmapuran:220:72	There one should make four vessels with sesame, perfume and water: three for the ancestors and one for the ghost, Brahmins.
brahmapuran:220:73	In the three vessels he should pour arghya from the ghost's vessel, reciting Ye samanah," and do the rest as before.
For women too it is thus: Ekoddishta is declared; Sapindikarana for them does not exist if there is no son.
Ekoddishta should be done by men for a woman every year, and on the day of death for the ancestors as prescribed.
In the absence of a son, the sapindas; in their absence, brothers of the same womb should properly do this rite; and a son's sons.
A maiden's son should do it for his maternal grandfathers; those called Dvyamushyayana should
worship the maternal grandfather and grandfather duly by occasional shraddhas also. In the absence of all, women should do it for their husbands without mantras.
In their absence, the king should have all rites such as cremation done properly for those without family by men of their own class.
For the king is the kinsman of all varnas. These have been told to you, Brahmins, the regular and occasional.
I shall tell of another rite based on shraddha, regular and occasional. Darsha (new moon) is the occasion there; know it with the waning of the moon.
The regular one has a fixed time; one should do it then as said. After Sapindikarana, the father's great-grandfather
goes to the eaters of smearings, cut off from the pinda of the ancestors; the fourth of them becomes an eater of smearings.
He too obtains a lesser enjoyment by connection. Father, grandfather and great-grandfather
these three persons are to be known as pinda-connected; others from the grandfather's grandfather onward are lepa-connected;
three are named of them, and the sacrificer is the seventh. Thus the connection of seven persons is told by the sages.
From the sacrificer upward there are the anulepa eaters; then all other earlier-born, those who dwell in hells,
those who have attained animal birth, those who stand in the state of ghosts and the like — the sacrificer performing shraddha by rule,
that one satisfies them, Brahmins, by whatever I now tell: the scattering of food done by men on the ground
satisfies those who have become pisachas. The water that falls on the ground from bathing clothes, Brahmins,
by it satisfaction arises for those who attained tree-hood. The drops of perfumed water that fall on the ground's surface
give nourishment to those who went to god-hood in the family. And the drops of water on the ground after the pindas are lifted
give nourishment to those who in the family went to animal-hood, and the toothless children in the family excluded from rites,
the dead without rights, who eat swept water; and the water of those who have eaten and rinsed, and what water arises from washing feet,
of Brahmins likewise — by this they go to satisfaction. Thus whatever sprinkling of water and food there is by the sacrificer and those Brahmins,
pure or leavings, by that food in the family those who have gone to another womb
go to nourishment, Brahmins, of those who properly perform shraddha. The shraddha done by men with wealth unjustly earned
does not satisfy those in the wombs of Chandalas, Pulkasas and the like. Thus nourishment of many through kinsmen, Brahmins,
arises here from those performing shraddha, by sprinklings of water. Therefore a man should perform shraddha with devotion, even with greens, by rule;
in the family of one who does shraddha no one sinks. Shraddha should be given to Brahmins who are self-controlled, keepers of Agnihotra,
of pure conduct, learned, especially Shrotriyas: one who knows Triṇāciketa, Trimadhu, Trisuparna, the six limbs,
devoted to mother and father, a sister's son, a knower of Samaveda; one should feed priests, house-priests, teachers and instructors,
maternal uncle, father-in-law, brother-in-law, relative, a reciter of Drona, a Mandala Brahmin who is skilled in the meaning of the Puranas,
one not following the ritual yet content with it, who refuses gifts: these Brahmins who purify a row are to be engaged at shraddha.
One should invite the previously mentioned best of Brahmins the previous day, and arrange them for the divine and ancestral assignments in the same way.
One who will perform the shraddha must be self-controlled; one who, having given or eaten at shraddha, has intercourse,
his ancestors lie in that semen for a month; one who goes to a woman or eats at a shraddha,
their ancestors for that month eat semen and urine as food; therefore the invitation should be made by the wise not at first.
If not available, or on that day, those devoted to women should be avoided. And the ascetics who come for alms, controlled, in time,
he should feed, appeased with prostration and the like, with attentive mind; the wise man should feed yogis too at shraddha then.
For ancestors have yoga as their support; therefore one should always worship them. If there is one yogi among thousands of Brahmins,
he would carry across the sacrificer and the eaters like a boat on water. Here the Brahman-speakers also sing an ancestors' verse:
the verse sung earlier by the ancestors of King Aila: "When will there be among our offspring a chief, some son
who on earth will give us pindas left over by yogis' food, or at Gaya a pinda, rhinoceros meat and oblation,
kalashaka greens, sesame and ghee, and krisara for our satisfaction, Vishvedeva and Soma (offerings), rhinoceros meat as the best oblation?
Without horns, from head to foot we bless;" one should give shraddha on the thirteenth, and under the Magha star, by rule.
Rice-pudding joined with honey and ghee in the southern course; therefore a man should worship his ancestors with devotion by rule,
wishing all desires and release of himself from sin. Vasus, Rudras, Adityas, stars, planets and stars
are pleased, ancestors satisfied by shraddha, and they give men long life, offspring, wealth, learning, heaven, liberation and pleasures;
the ancestors, satisfied by shraddha, give kingdom also. Thus the afternoon exceeds the forenoon for ancestors.
Having worshipped those twice-born who have come to one's house with welcome, he should seat them on seats, their hands purified and having rinsed.
Having done shraddha by rule and fed the best of Brahmins, he should dismiss them speaking pleasantly and bowing with devotion.
He should follow them to the door, and return with permission; then he should do the daily rite and feed guests.
Some, best of men, want the daily rite of ancestors; others not so; one should do the rest as before.
Others say separately; some say earlier as before; then the man should eat that food with servants and others.
Thus the knower of dharma, composed, should do the ancestral shraddha so that satisfaction arises in the chief Brahmins.
Now I shall tell the lowest of the twice-born to be avoided: betrayer of a friend, one with bad nails, impotent, consumptive, one with white (leprosy), trader on the road,
one with dark teeth, bald, one-eyed, blind, deaf, dull, dumb, lame, crippled, eunuch, one with bad skin, deformed, squinting,
leper, red-eyed, hunchback, dwarf, ugly, lazy, enemy of friend, of bad family, cowherd, shapeless,
a younger brother married before the elder, the elder who is unmarried, son of the woman married as a second wife, husband of a low-caste woman and her son — a Brahmin should not be a shraddha eater.
The performer of rites for a low-caste woman's son, an unmarried one, husband of a widow, a paid teacher, one taught by pay,
one living on food of impurity, hunter, soma-seller, falsely accused, thief, fallen, usurer, rogue,
informer, abandoner of the Veda, harsh in abandoning gifts and fires, the king's priest, servant, one devoid of learning, envious,
hater of elders, difficult, cruel, foolish, temple-priest, star-reader, and the despised festival-maker,
priest for those unfit for sacrifice, eunuch, those despised and the lowest: these should not be engaged at shraddha, seen as defilers of the row.
Where the bad are favoured and the good insulted, there divine punishment, terrible, falls at once.
One who, abandoning the well-ordained scripture, feeds a fool, abandoning the primal dharma — the giver there perishes.
One who, abandoning a Brahmin who depends on him, brings another and feeds him, the giver there perishes, burnt by the fire of that one's sighs.
Without clothing there is no rite, no sacrifice, Vedas or austerities; therefore garments should be given, especially at the time of shraddha.
Silk, linen, cotton, undamaged fine cloth: one who gives these at shraddha obtains excellent desires.
As among many cows a calf finds its mother, so food finds its way there where the creature stays through the Brahmins.
Name, gotra and mantras convey the food given even to those who have died; satisfaction reaches them.
Salutation to gods, to ancestors and to great yogis; to Svaha and Svadha; may it be always so.
One should recite this three times at the beginning and end of shraddha, and also concentrated at the offering of pindas.
The ancestors come quickly and Rakshasas flee; they are pleased in the three worlds; this mantra saves.
One should give new linen thread, hemp and cotton, and avoid leaf-wool, silk thread and silk;
the wise should avoid the fringeless, even if unharmed; these do not please, and there would be harm to the giver.
A pinda should not be offered to ancestors by one whose father is living; he should feed him by rule with desired food and eatables.
A man desiring enjoyment should always give a pinda in fire; desiring offspring he should give the middle one to his wife with a mantra.
Desiring excellent lustre one gives the pinda to cows; and wisdom, fame and renown one offers in water.
Praying for long life one gives to crows; desiring a school for boys one gives to cocks.
Some Brahmins say that the pinda is to be lifted first; with those Brahmins' permission, let it be lifted as desired.
Therefore shraddha should be done as said formerly by the sages; otherwise there is fault and it does not reach the ancestors.
